Second Schleswig War: War between Denmark, Prussia, and Austria in 1864.

Formed in 2022 after a leadership split within a major Maharashtra party, this faction led by former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray was given a new 'Flaming Torch' symbol by India's Election Commission — which party?
Shiv Sena (UBT): Political party in Maharashtra, India. Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) (ISO: Śiva Sēnā (Uddhava Bāḷāsāhēba Ṭhākare); lit. 'Army of Shivaji, led by Uddhav Thackeray'; abbr.
Sparked in 1898 by the sinking of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor, this brief conflict handed the U.S. control of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines — what was it?
Spanish–American War: 1898 conflict between Spain and the United States.
Active from 1973 to 1975, this American far-left militant group kidnapped newspaper heiress Patty Hearst and had six members die in a 1974 Los Angeles shootout with police — which group?
Symbionese Liberation Army: American militant organization (1973–1975). The three surviving fugitives recruited new members, but nearly all of them were apprehended in 1975 and prosecuted.

Published by Anton LaVey in 1969, this text serves as the foundational scripture of a philosophy whose adherents describe themselves as 'atheistic' believers who see supernatural figures as projections of personality — which book?
The Satanic Bible: 1969 religious text of LaVeyan Satanism.
This movement campaigns for women to have the same legal right as men to go bare-chested in public, and also supports mothers' right to breastfeed openly — which cause?
Topfreedom: Social movement to allow female toplessness.
The son of Ivan III and Sophia Paleologue, this Grand Prince of Moscow annexed Pskov and Ryazan and captured Smolensk from Lithuania during his reign from 1505 to 1533 — who was he?
Vasili III of Russia: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1505 to 1533.
As East Germany's chief decision-maker for two decades, this communist leader demanded the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 despite Soviet reluctance — who was he?
Walter Ulbricht: Leader of East Germany from 1950 to 1971.
The New York Times once called him the country's best-known lawyer; this civil rights attorney is most famous for defending the Chicago Seven — who is it?
Harold Alexander, 1st Earl Alexander of Tunis
William Kunstler: American attorney and civil rights activist (1919–1995)
A Russian lawyer-turned-politician who chaired the Duma's Family, Women and Children Affairs committee, she drew attention in 2012 for drafting controversial LGBT-related legislation — who is she?
Created in 1946 and headquartered in Paris, this government-owned utility operates 56 nuclear reactors across 18 sites and was the world's largest electricity producer in 2009 — which company?
Électricité de France: French multinational electric utility company.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four. Originally specified in the late 1950s, it is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in common use, after Fortran.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Roger Joseph Boscovich is a physicist.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Percy Lavon Julian is a chemist. Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899 – April 19, 1975) was an American research chemist and a pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants.
What is the atomic number of Mendelevium?
Mendelevium: Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
In what year was Grigori Perelman born?
Grigori Perelman: The full details of Perelman's work were filled in and explained by various authors over the following several years.
In what year was Sean Parker born?
Sean Parker: According to Forbes, as of May 2025, Parker's estimated net worth stood at US$3.0 billion, placing him in the top 1,250 richest individuals in the world.
In what year was C. V. Raman born?
C. V. Raman: This phenomenon, a hitherto unknown type of scattering of light they called modified scattering, was subsequently termed the Raman effect or Raman scattering.
In what year did Hypatia die?
Hypatia: Not the only fourth century Alexandrian female mathematician, Hypatia was preceded by Pandrosion.
In what year did Jan Hus die?
Jan Hus: Hus is considered to be the first Church reformer, even though some designate the theorist John Wycliffe.
In what year was Radium discovered?
Radium: Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
In what year was Copper discovered?
Copper: Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu (from Latin cuprum) and atomic number 29.
Mil Mi-17: Kazan Helicopters. It is known as the Mi-8M series in Russian service.
Which country is Curtiss P-40 Warhawk from?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk: United States. The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
Who is credited with discovering Ruthenium?
Ruthenium: Karl Ernst Claus. Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
Who is credited with discovering Aniline?
Aniline: Otto Unverdorben. Aniline (From Portuguese: anil, meaning 'indigo shrub', and -ine indicating a derived substance) is an organic compound with the formula C6H5NH2.
Who is credited with discovering Lie group?
Lie group: Sophus Lie. Combining these two ideas, one obtains a continuous group where multiplying points and their inverses is continuous.
With the formula (CH3)2CO, this volatile solvent is produced by the millions of tonnes yearly, much of it to make precursors for plastics like bisphenol A — what is it?
Acetone (2-propanone or dimethyl ketone) is an organic compound with the formula (CH3)2CO.
A close relative of the peach in the genus Prunus, this drupe's seed isn't a true nut and can be "blanched" by softening its skin in hot water before peeling — what is it?
These eusocial insects evolved from vespoid wasps back in the Cretaceous, and you can spot one by its elbowed antennae and pinched, node-like waist. Which creature is it?
Ant are eusocial insects of the family Formicidae and, along with the related wasps and bees, belong to the order Hymenoptera.
The second-largest living lizard species after the Komodo dragon, native to South and Southeast Asia. It's a varanid found from India to the Indonesian islands. What is it?
Asian water monitor (Varanus salvator) is a large varanid lizard native to South and Southeast Asia.
Causing frequent urination and a weak stream, this noncancerous enlargement of a male gland isn't caused by poor hygiene and has no known cure, only symptom management. What condition is it?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), also called prostate enlargement, is a noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.

This semi-solid tissue inside the spongy portions of bones serves as the primary site of new blood cell production in birds and mammals, making up roughly 5% of an adult human's body mass — what tissue is it?
Bone marrow is a semi-solid tissue found within the spongy (also known as cancellous) portions of bones.

What suborder of orthopteran insects — its Latin name meaning 'chisel-bearing,' after the stout shape of its members' egg-laying organs — includes grasshoppers, ground-hoppers, and pygmy mole crickets?
Caelifera are a suborder of orthopteran insects. The latter should not be confused with the mole crickets (Gryllotalpidae), which belong to the other Orthopteran suborder Ensifera.

Derived from the amino acid tyrosine and fifty percent bound to plasma proteins in your bloodstream, what class of neurotransmitter has a benzene ring topped with two hydroxyl groups plus a side-chain amine?

Catecholamine (abbreviated CA), most typically a 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine, is a monoamine neurotransmitter, an organic compound that has a catechol (benzene with two hydroxyl side groups next to each other) and a side-chain amine.
Most species of this loud insect superfamily emerge annually, but a few North American ones famously emerge en masse only once every several years. What insects are they?
Cicada are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
Known by a colorful nickname, this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye turns it pink, may leave it stuck shut by morning, and spreads easily — what is it?
Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
A law professor known for scholarship on retribution and criminal sentencing, this Harvard-trained academic was killed in 2014 in a murder-for-hire scheme linked to a custody dispute — who is he?

Dan Markel (October 9, 1972 - July 19, 2014) was a Canadian-born attorney and law professor who wrote various works on retribution in criminal law and sentencing with a focus on the role of punishment in the criminal justice system.
A member of the catecholamine family made by stripping a carboxyl group from L-DOPA, this brain chemical is central to reward-motivated behavior — what is it?
Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
This is the earliest developmental stage of a multicellular organism, beginning with a single-celled zygote formed just after fertilization — what is it called?
Embryo is the initial stage of development for a multicellular organism.
This term describes the practice of exposing normally covered body parts to others in public or semi-public settings, whether in person or via a nude photo shared digitally — what is it?
Exhibitionism is the practice of exposing one's intimate parts - such as the breasts, genitals, or buttocks - in a public or semi-public environment.
Sharing the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Maurice Wilkins, this English molecular biologist helped decipher the structure of DNA — who is he?
Francis Crick (8 June 1916 - 28 July 2004) was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist.

Built from epithelial tissue with a supporting connective-tissue capsule, this kind of structure secretes hormones straight into the blood if it's ductless, or through a duct to a cavity or surface if not — what is it called?
Gland is a cell or an organ in an animal's body that produces and secretes different substances that the organism needs, either into the bloodstream or into a body cavity or outer surface.
This perception occurs with no external stimulus at all, yet feels completely real to the person experiencing it — distinct from dreaming, illusions, or ordinary imagination — name this phenomenon?
Hallucination is a perception in the absence of an external context stimulus that has the compelling sense of reality.
Nesting monogamously in tree cavities across Africa, Asia, and Melanesia, these birds are unique for having their first two neck vertebrae fused solid — which birds?
Hornbill are birds found in tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and Melanesia of the family Bucerotidae.
Supplied by the lumbar spinal nerves and part of the femoral nerve, this fused pair of abdominal and thigh muscles is the body's strongest hip flexor — what is it called?
Iliopsoas (from Latin ile 'groin' and Ancient Greek (ps) 'muscles of the loins') refers to the joined psoas major and the iliacus muscles.
Most of the flowers used by the global perfume industry for this fragrant genus of shrubs and vines are grown in a single Egyptian village. What plant is it?
Jasmine (botanical name: Jasminum) is a genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family of Oleaceae.

This childhood illness of unknown cause mainly affects kids under five, causing a prolonged fever lasting more than five days that doesn't respond to typical fever-reducing medicine, plus inflamed blood vessels throughout the body — name the syndrome?
Kawasaki disease (also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is a syndrome of unknown cause that results in a fever and mainly affects children under 5 years of age.

A Cornell-trained engineer and Atlanta factory superintendent, this man was wrongly convicted of a young employee's murder, then kidnapped from prison and lynched in a case now central to American antisemitism — who was he?

Leo Frank (April 17, 1884 - August 17, 1915) was an American lynching victim wrongly convicted of the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan, an employee in a factory in Atlanta, Georgia, where he was the superintendent.
Credited as the 'Father of Cinematography' for filming Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888, this French inventor mysteriously vanished in 1890 before cinema took off — who was he?

Louis Le Prince (28 August 1841 - disappeared 16 September 1890; declared dead 16 September 1897) was a French artist and the inventor of an early motion-picture camera, and director of Roundhay Garden Scene.
Sharing the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on nuclear shell structure, this German-American theorist became only the second woman ever to win that prize, after Marie Curie — who was she?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (ne Goppert; June 28, 1906 - February 20, 1972) was a German-American theoretical physicist who shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics with J. Hans D. Jensen.
Ranked among the world's wealthiest people as of 2026, this billionaire founded and still leads a technology infrastructure giant he once took private in a landmark buyout — who is he?
Michael Dell (born February 23, 1965) is an American billionaire businessman and investor.
An Austrian-School economist who called the state 'robbery systematized and writ large,' he founded and championed anarcho-capitalism across more than twenty books — who was he?
Murray Rothbard (March 2, 1926 - January 7, 1995) was an American economist of the Austrian School, economic historian, political theorist, and activist.

Found across 26 African countries in lakes, rivers and swamps — with one of its largest undisturbed populations at Kenya's Lake Turkana — adult males of this reptile can stretch past five meters; what is it?
Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) is a large crocodilian native to freshwater habitats in Africa, where it is present in 26 countries.
Listed by Ptolemy and named for a hunter in Greek myth, this winter constellation boasts the supergiant stars Rigel and Betelgeuse and a famous short, straight line of three stars — which is it?
Orion (constellation) is a prominent set of stars visible during winter in the northern celestial hemisphere.
First domesticated in Neolithic China and rarely living past twenty years, this deciduous fruit tree also produces a smooth-skinned variety commercially sold as a different fruit — which tree?
Peach (Prunus persica) is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics.

This class of lipid molecules has a water-loving 'head' built around a phosphate group and two water-fearing fatty-acid 'tails' — and forms an essential building block of neuronal membranes in the brain. Name the class of molecule?

Phospholipid are a class of lipids whose molecule has a hydrophilic "head" containing a phosphate group and two hydrophobic "tails" derived from fatty acids, joined by an alcohol residue (usually a glycerol molecule).
Though it looks like a small dolphin, this cetacean is actually more closely related to narwhals and belugas, and can be told apart by its flattened, spade-shaped teeth — what animal is it?
Porpoise are small dolphin-like cetaceans classified under the family Phocoenidae.
This yellow-white fluid forms at sites of infection and inflammation — when trapped in tissue it's called an abscess, and near the skin's surface a pimple — name the substance?
Pus is an exudate, typically white-yellow, yellow, or yellow-brown, formed at the site of inflammation during infections, regardless of cause.
Named from Greek words for 'rose' and 'tree,' this genus of over 1,000 woody flowering plant species serves as the national flower of Nepal and the state flower of Washington — what is it?

Rhododendron (pl.: rhododendra), from Ancient Greek (rhdon), meaning "rose", and (dndron), meaning "tree", is a very large genus of about 1,024 species of woody plants in the heath family (Ericaceae).
Also known as Besnier-Boeck-Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition causes inflammatory cell clusters called granulomata, most often striking the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis is a non-infectious granulomatous disease involving abnormal collections of inflammatory cells that form lumps known as granulomata.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

This now-discredited scientific theory held that living creatures like fleas or maggots could regularly arise directly from non-living matter such as dust or rotting flesh, and was coherently synthesized by Aristotle. Name the theory?
Spontaneous generation is a superseded scientific theory that held that living creatures could arise from non-living matter and that such processes were commonplace and regular.
Time named this marine biologist its first "Hero for the Planet" in 1998, the same year she became a National Geographic Explorer — and she was also NOAA's first chief scientist. Who is she?
Sylvia Earle (born August 30, 1935) is an American marine biologist, oceanographer, explorer, writer, and lecturer.
Raised by a wealthy uncle after his father fled following a fight, this English philosopher laid out an influential social contract theory in his 1651 book 'Leviathan' — who is he?

Thomas Hobbes (HOBZ; 5 April 1588 - 4 December 1679) was an English philosopher and political theorist, best known for his 1651 book Leviathan, in which he expounds an influential formulation of social contract theory.
Native to Central and South America but now found in sub-Saharan Africa, which parasitic flea burrows into skin to cause the condition tungiasis?
Tunga penetrans is a species of flea also known as the jigger, jigger flea, chigoe, chigo, chigoe flea, chigo flea, nigua, sand flea, or burrowing flea.

Commanding the first spaceflight to carry multiple crew members in 1964, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first human to die during a space mission when his capsule's parachute failed on reentry in 1967 — who was he?
Vladimir Komarov (16 March 1927 - 24 April 1967) was a Soviet test pilot, aerospace engineer, and cosmonaut.
Which East Asian citrus fruit, believed to have originated in central China as a hybrid of mandarin orange and ichang papeda, is now also grown in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe?
Yuzu (Citrus junos, from Japanese or) is a citrus fruit and plant in the family Rutaceae of Chinese origin.
Native to Africa and Yemen, this drought-resistant tree species has individuals radiocarbon-dated to over 1,275 years old — what is it?
Adansonia digitata: Species of plant native to Africa.
Brother of a concert pianist and son of an astronomer, this Russian mathematician built the foundational theory of stability in dynamical systems — who was he?
Formed when ammonia gains an extra hydrogen ion, this positively charged molecule, NH4+, is a key player in the global nitrogen cycle — what is it?
Caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, its skin form starts as a small blister that becomes a painless ulcer with a telltale black center — what infection is this?
Anthrax: Infection caused by Bacillus anthracis bacteria. The skin form presents with a small blister with surrounding swelling that often turns into a painless ulcer with a black center.
Painting, sculpture, and architecture are its three classical visual branches, yet nobody can agree on a single definition for it; what cultural pursuit of creative and imaginative talent is this?
Art: Creative work to evoke aesthetic response.
The world's largest nocturnal primate, this Madagascar lemur has ever-growing rodent-like teeth and taps tree trunks with a bony middle finger to fish out grubs by echo — which animal?
Aye-aye: Species of primate. This foraging method is called percussive foraging, and takes up 5–41% of the aye-aye's foraging time.
Named after the aromatic resin from which it was first derived, this simplest aromatic carboxylic compound forms salts widely used as food preservatives — what is it called?
Believed to descend from hounds once kept at a Belgian abbey, this scent hound can follow a human trail days old and is a favorite of police tracking escaped prisoners — which breed is it?
Bloodhound: Dog breed used for tracking by scent.
Grown on one of the Amazon's largest and longest-lived trees, this selenium-rich edible seed comes in a shell weighing up to 2 kilograms combined with its fruit. What is it?
Brazil nut: Species of tree and its edible seeds.
Native to tropical Africa, this gourd-producing vine yields fruit that can be eaten young as a vegetable or dried and hollowed out into bowls, ladles, or even musical instruments — what is it?
Calabash: Species of bottle gourd plant.
Ranked the world's richest person by Forbes from 2010 to 2013, this Mexican tycoon built his fortune largely through telecommunications and remains Latin America's wealthiest individual — who is he?
Around 20 millimetres long with a shimmering structural-green shell and a coppery underside, this beetle is identified by its isosceles-triangle scutellum — which species?
Cetonia aurata: Species of beetle. The scutellum is the small V-shaped area between the wing cases; it may show several small, irregular, white lines and marks.
This human-feeding ectoparasite is one of the world's great "nuisance pests" — yet despite carrying dozens of pathogens, no study has shown it transmits any disease to us. What is it?
Cimex lectularius: Species of true bug.
This umbrella term covers mental processes like perception, attention, memory, and reasoning that let us acquire and apply knowledge — what is it called?
Cognition: Mental process dealing with knowledge.
Born in 1863, this Italian is remembered as a major contributor to the early development of algebraic geometry — who was he?
This herpesvirus genus's human species can cause mononucleosis in adults but birth defects affecting the eyes, ears, liver, and spleen when passed to a fetus — which virus?
Cytomegalovirus: Genus of viruses. The 11 species in this genus include Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV, HHV-5), which is the species that infects humans.
Marked by up to 20 liters of dilute urine a day and intense thirst that drinking barely satisfies, this condition comes in four types tied to problems with the hormone vasopressin — what is it?
Diabetes insipidus: Condition characterized by large amounts of dilute urine and increased thirst.
Working alongside biochemist Katalin Karikó on nucleoside base modifications, this University of Pennsylvania immunologist shared the 2023 Nobel Prize for enabling COVID-19 mRNA vaccines — who is he?
Drew Weissman: American physician and immunologist (born 1959)
Named for the large trunk-like proboscis of its males, this giant oceangoing pinniped can weigh up to 4,000 kilograms and was once hunted nearly to extinction for lamp oil. What animal is it?
Elephant seal: Genus of aquatic carnivores.
Sold under the brand name Nexium, this proton pump inhibitor treats acid reflux by blocking an enzyme in the stomach's acid-producing cells — what is it?
Esomeprazole: Medication which reduces stomach acid.
Co-founder and CEO of Snap Inc., this businessman was the youngest billionaire in the world back in 2015 — who is he?

Boldly patterned in black and yellow to warn predators of its toxicity, this European amphibian can live for more than 50 years and is now vulnerable due to an introduced fungal disease — what species is it?
Fire salamander: Species of amphibian. The fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) is a common species of salamander found in Europe.
Often bonded to glucose to form sucrose, this simple sugar is found in honey, fruit, and most root vegetables — which sugar?
Fructose: Simple ketonic monosaccharide found in many plants.
Named from Greek words for 'old man' and 'healer,' this medical specialty focuses on preventing and treating disease in older adults with no fixed age cutoff — what is it called?
Geriatrics: Medical specialty that focuses on health care of elderly people.
This cluster of immune cells forms around bacteria, fungi, or foreign material the body can't otherwise clear away — what is it called?
Granuloma: Inflammatory aggregation of immune cells.

This British aviation entrepreneur held three Guinness World Records after visiting the South Pole, the Challenger Deep, and space, then died in 2023 aboard the submersible that imploded near the Titanic wreck — who was he?
Some called egrets and others bitterns, these 75 species of long-legged, long-beaked wading birds make up the family Ardeidae — what are they?
Heron: Family of birds. The OED also observes that shiterow or shederow are terms used for herons, and also applied as derogatory terms meaning a thin, weakly person.
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor. It is a simple pnictogen hydride, and is a colourless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odour.
The world's largest jet airliner when it first flew in 1963, this Soviet quad-engine jetliner entered Aeroflot service with a Moscow-to-Montreal flight in 1967. What aircraft?
Ilyushin Il-62: Soviet long-range narrow-body four-engined jet airliner.
An Indian polymath and pioneer of radio microwave optics, he's also considered the father of Bengali science fiction — and even has a crater on the Moon named for him. Who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose: Physicist, biologist and botanist (1857–1937)
On January 26, 1926, this Scottish inventor gave the world's first demonstration of a working mechanical television system — who is he?
Derived from Greek words for 'movement' and 'study,' this scientific field examines biomechanics, motor control, and rehabilitation to understand how the human body moves — what field is this?
Kinesiology: Study of human body movement. Kinesiology addresses physiological, anatomical, biomechanical, pathological, neuropsychological principles and mechanisms of movement.
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element honors the man who invented the cyclotron — the very machine used to discover so many artificial elements. Which element is it?
Lawrencium: Chemical element with atomic number 103 (Lr)
Named in honor of a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of bacteria causes a rare but serious foodborne illness with a fatality rate up to 30 percent — what is it?
Listeria: Genus of bacteria. Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Named from a Greek root meaning 'light' or 'brightness' in reference to its luminous, reflective eyes, this genus includes the bobcat among its four wild cat species — which genus?
Lynx: Genus of medium-sized wild cats.
A Russian pediatric endocrinologist also known by the surname Faassen, this woman is the elder child of Russia's president. Who is she?
Maria Vorontsova: Daughter of Vladimir Putin (born 1985)
Also called pennyroyal, this minty flowering plant native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East has a folk-remedy history despite being toxic to the liver — what species is it?
This twin-engine Soviet fighter, known to NATO as 'Fulcrum,' was built in the 1970s to counter American jets like the F-15 and F-16 — which aircraft is it?
Mikoyan MiG-29: Soviet twin-engine jet fighter aircraft. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.

First identified from skulls found in a Dutch chalk quarry near Maastricht and initially mistaken for crocodile or whale bones, this giant marine lizard genus lived until 66 million years ago — which genus is it?
Mosasaurus: Extinct genus of marine lizard from the Late Cretaceous.
Divided in two by a central septum, this air-filled space sits behind the nose and forms the uppermost part of the respiratory system — what is it?
Nasal cavity: Large, air-filled space above and behind the nose in the middle of the face.
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American is regarded as the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines — who was he?
Norbert Wiener: American mathematician and philosopher (1894–1964)

Found above 3,500 metres on the Tibetan Plateau, this parasitic fungus grows out of moth larvae and is prized — despite containing arsenic — as an aphrodisiac in traditional Chinese medicine. What is it commonly called?
Ophiocordyceps sinensis: Species of fungus. It parasitizes larvae of ghost moths and produces a fruiting body which is valued in traditional Chinese medicine and Nepalese medicine as an aphrodisiac.
From a single western-Mediterranean flowering plant come both a notorious drug and the tiny dark seeds sprinkled on your bagel — which species is it?
Papaver somniferum: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family.
A hybrid cross of watermint and spearmint, this herb is one of the oldest used in cooking and medicine and a key plant source of menthol — what is it?
Peppermint: Hybrid flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Enclosed in a papery husk derived from its calyx, this nightshade genus includes the tomatillo and Cape gooseberry among its edible-fruited species — which genus?

The most common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age, it's diagnosed by two of three signs — irregular periods, high testosterone, or many antral follicles — despite a name that misleadingly implies true cysts. What's its newer name?
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: Hormonal disorder in women. The exact cause of PMOS remains uncertain.
Native to Eurasia and known by the common names 'cherry plum' and 'myrobalan plum,' this species is thought to be a parent of the cultivated plum — what is it, scientifically?
Prunus cerasifera: Species of plum. Native to Eurasia and naturalized elsewhere, P. cerasifera is believed to be one of the parents of the cultivated plum.
Built from bases including uracil, adenine, guanine, and cytosine, this molecule can serve as a template for building proteins or catalyze reactions itself — what is it?
RNA: Family of large biological molecules.
This branch of medicine handles more than 100 inflammatory diseases of the bones, muscles, and joints — like lupus and arthritis — and overlaps heavily with immunology. What is it?
Rheumatology: Medical speciality of inflammatory diseases.
Known as 'swede' in British English, this root vegetable is a hybrid of cabbage and turnip — what is it?
Rutabaga: Root vegetable in the Brassica family.
Usually forming an S- or C-shaped curve with a rotational twist, this sideways irregular curvature of the spine sits alongside kyphosis and lordosis among the spine's abnormal curves. What is it?
Scoliosis: Left-right asymmetry of the spine's curvature.
This Japanese army medical officer led a biological and chemical warfare unit in Japanese-occupied Manchuria during World War II and was later granted immunity — who is he?
Shirō Ishii: Japanese biological weapons specialist (1892–1959)
Famous for a repetitive, melodic call often referenced in poetry, this brown, spotted-breasted bird uses a favorite stone as an 'anvil' to crack open snail shells — which species?
Song thrush: Species of bird. The song thrush (Turdus philomelos) is a thrush that breeds across the West Palearctic.
Fired by Apple's board in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought a animation studio before returning a decade later to revolutionize consumer tech. Who?
Steve Jobs: American businessman and inventor (1955–2011)
Serving as prime minister of Turkey seven separate times before becoming president from 1993 to 2000, he was also the first PM to have been born in the Turkish Republic — who was he?

Süleyman Demirel: President of Turkey from 1993 to 2000. Demirel was the leader of the opposition from 1971 to 1975 before forming a right-wing government known as the First Nationalist Front, which collapsed in 1977.
